title: The Influence of Forest Resting Environments on Stress Using Virtual Reality
research_question: To explore the effects of different types of forest resting environments on human stress levels and to compare their health benefits from the perspective of stress relief.

participants.description: 96 college students and social workers (33 males, 63 females), average age 24.03 ± 5.29 years old, right-handed, normal or corrected normal vision, no mental/stress/organic/endocrine diseases, from Beijing, China.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Seven distinct 5-minute VR videos of forest resting environments, filmed in 33 forest parks in Beijing. Environments varied in artificialization, presence of water, and specific landscape elements (e.g., wooden pavilion, plants, benches, platforms, waterfall, pool).

mechanisms: The presence of many plants and other natural factors in VR videos contributes to stress relief.
Environments with rich content might have a better effect on relieving stress.
The 'refuge' characteristic of an environment might play an important role in psychological stress relief.
implementation_implications: The conclusions of this study are conducive to the better use of the forest environment for forest therapy services.

Understanding health benefits of different forest environments is crucial for transforming the forest environment, carrying out forest therapy activities, and giving the public a choice of recuperation sites.
Forest rest requires the use and transformation of the environment to better utilize the resource advantages of the forest.
The development of forest therapy activities requires more in-depth theoretical support so that the forest can be better utilized.
A water landscape, especially a dynamic one, can play a good role in relieving stress both physically and psychologically.

limitations: Only seven types of forest resting environments were explored, which were a summary of a survey in Beijing, and future research should expand to more diverse types.
The essential reasons for the different stress-relieving effects were not found; the internal mechanism was not established.
The theoretical background for selecting the seven environments was not sufficient, as the quoted PSD theory was not very compatible with the environments.
The stress relief effect of water landscape showed complexity and seems to be affected by many factors, requiring further exploration.

Indicators need further improvement; salivary amylase concentration increased to a certain extent, which was inconsistent with previous studies, possibly due to small sample size or VR video distortion. Heart rate variability (HRV) should be added.
The fixed visual angle of the VR video might cause aesthetic fatigue, and VR experience is not the same as real environment exposure, suggesting future field experiments.
Only visual factors were focused on, ignoring other senses (hearing, smell, taste, touch) and environmental factors (air quality, temperature, humidity).
Specific activities for 'forest rests' were ignored, and different activities (meditation, body scanning, walking, painting) could affect stress relief.
Most participants were undergraduate students and may not be representative of the general public; the number of participants needs to be increased.

environmental_features: virtual forest environment (visuals and sounds of nature)
virtual urban environment (visuals and sounds of city traffic)

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Natural environments facilitate recovery from directed attention fatigue and stress by providing 'being away', 'fascination', 'extent', and 'compatibility'.
Exposure to natural environments promotes physiological and psychological stress reduction more effectively than urban environments.
